tier_reason: The suite meets A methodology (public harness src/tests/vincenthzlibjsontest.cpp and src/tests/nlohmanntest.cpp, clang 7.0, premake5 optimize Full + -march=native, Core i7-4980HQ), but every libjson row that beats nlohmann/json times benchmark-written code with correctness bugs: tree_print ignores its print_func argument and always calls json_print_raw, so the Prettify row produces compact output, and it emits JSON false and null as quoted strings, so the citm_catalog.json and twitter.json Stringify output is wrong. The one row that exercises libjson's own parser against nlohmann (Parse) is slower, so the bug-in-measured-path rule caps it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Against nlohmann/json v2.0.3, sum of the three files (derived from page data): Stringify 68.767 ms vs 87.732 ms (about 1.28x); per file canada.json 61.512 vs 76.315 ms, citm_catalog.json 4.067 vs 7.178 ms, twitter.json 3.188 vs 4.239 ms. These rows time a benchmark-written tree printer: numbers are formatted by the harness with sprintf("%.17g") or "%lld" (libjson does no number conversion), and false/null are printed as quoted strings, so only the canada.json row (no null or false values) produces correct output. The Prettify row (69.279 vs 130.560 ms) is not a valid comparison: the harness never calls json_print_pretty, so libjson emits the same compact text as in Stringify (same time and the same 5.24 MB) while nlohmann runs dump(4). The Statistics row (0.803 vs 2.171 ms) walks the harness's own tree, not libjson code. Parse, the only row using libjson's parser to build a tree, is slower than nlohmann: 107.172 vs 72.476 ms (about 0.68x; canada 77.479 vs 55.591, citm 20.334 vs 9.875, twitter 9.359 vs 7.010 ms); it beats JsonCpp 1.0.0 (165.522 ms, about 1.54x) and json-c 0.12.1 (134.551 ms, about 1.26x) on the totals only because of canada.json (all derived from page data). Parse memory 8.59 MB vs nlohmann 9.90 MB (derived) is the harness tree's footprint.

corrections.caveats: Harness flaws behind the numbers (src/tests/vincenthzlibjsontest.cpp, unchanged at HEAD): libjson has 'No object model integrated' (README), so the suite builds its own tree through json_parser_dom callbacks (tree_create_structure, tree_create_data, tree_append) and prints it with its own tree_print; tree_print ignores the json_print_pretty argument and always calls json_print_raw, so the Prettify row is compact output and the 1.88x prettify figure is void; tree_print emits JSON_FALSE and JSON_NULL as JSON_STRING, so twitter.json (2446 false, 1946 null) and citm_catalog.json (1263 null) are serialised wrongly; number formatting is harness sprintf. The Statistics win measures the harness tree. Parse, the row that exercises libjson, is 1.48x slower than nlohmann/json. libjson's own SAX rows have no nlohmann baseline (SAX round-trip 30.778 ms, SAX statistics 22.478 ms, versus RapidJSON 18.143 and 6.318 ms). Conformance in the same suite: 2 of 34 parse-validation, 9 of 66 double-parse and 10 of 27 round-trip tests fail (nlohmann fails 4 of 27 round-trip). The README's 'Fast: use efficient code and small parsing tables for maximum efficiency' has no numbers. Security note: json_parser_dom's dom_push realloc'd its stack without multiplying by the element size (heap overflow past 1024 nesting levels), fixed in e03b4a9 (2018-10-06) after the 2016 run; the test files never nest that deep. Sample results are dated 2016-09-09 and use 2016 library versions (nlohmann v2.0.3); today's ratios will differ. Per-library totals are sums of the three per-file rows and are derived from page data. LGPL-2.1-only OR LGPL-3.0-only (header in json.c; no LICENSE file).

notes: Every number matches the CSV rows 'Vinenthz/libjson (C)' and 'Nlohmann (C++11)', but the wins over nlohmann come from benchmark-written tree code with two correctness bugs (Prettify never pretty-prints; false/null written as strings), and libjson's own parse is slower, so A to C. Shortcomings to record: prettify row void (compact output), stringify output wrong for false/null on citm and twitter, statistics and number formatting are harness code, parse 1.48x slower than nlohmann, conformance failures, 2016 data, pre-2018 dom_push heap overflow. Metadata confirmed: 294 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-05-12.

tier_reason: Independent nativejson-benchmark: public harness (src/tests/parsontest.cpp calls json_parse_string; src/tests/jsoncpptest.cpp, jsonctest.cpp, nlohmanntest.cpp), clang 7.0 64-bit, build/premake5.lua release optimize Full, NDEBUG, -march=native, Core i7-4980HQ, so A holds for the parse claim against JsonCpp and json-c. Verdict is downgrade only because the claim included an invalid prettify comparison.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Parse, sum of the three files (derived from page data): Parson 89.549 ms vs JsonCpp 1.0.0 165.522 ms (about 1.85x), json-c 0.12.1 134.551 ms (about 1.50x) and Qt 5.6 QJsonDocument 124.957 ms (about 1.40x). The win is driven by canada.json (64.573 ms vs JsonCpp 142.458, json-c 105.784, Qt 114.775); on citm_catalog.json Parson (17.144 ms) is slower than JsonCpp (14.587) and Qt (7.052) and faster than json-c (21.122); on twitter.json (7.832 ms) it is faster than JsonCpp (8.477) and slower than json-c (7.645) and Qt (3.130). Parse memory 9.14 MB vs JsonCpp 24.56 MB and json-c 49.89 MB (derived; Qt allocations are not tracked), though Parson makes more allocations (594,122 vs JsonCpp 386,181). Stringify 110.903 ms is slower than nlohmann/json v2.0.3 (87.732), JsonCpp (94.261) and json-c (30.804) and faster only than Qt (152.185, about 1.37x, derived). There is no valid prettify comparison: the suite's Parson Prettify calls json_serialize_to_string (compact), so its 111.205 ms is not comparable with nlohmann's dump(4) 130.560 ms. Parse is slower than nlohmann/json (72.476 ms), cJSON (24.671) and RapidJSON (7.932).

corrections.caveats: Nobody claims Parson is fast: the README calls it lightweight and has no performance claim. The parse win over JsonCpp, json-c and Qt rests mostly on canada.json; on citm_catalog.json and twitter.json Parson loses to Qt and to one of JsonCpp/json-c. It loses to nlohmann/json, cJSON (24.671 ms parse total) and RapidJSON (7.932 ms), and its stringify is 3.6x slower than json-c (30.804 vs 110.903 ms). The suite's Prettify row for Parson calls the compact serializer, so the prettify 1.17x figure against nlohmann is void. Conformance in the same suite: 3 of 34 parse-validation, 1 of 9 string-parse and 13 of 27 round-trip tests fail. Library revision used in the sample is not stated, and the suite README's version table was edited after the run. Sample results are dated 2016-09-09 and use 2016 library versions; today's ratios will differ. Per-library totals are sums of the three per-file rows (canada.json 2199KB, citm_catalog.json 1737KB, twitter.json 632KB) and are derived from page data.

notes: All parse, stringify, memory and conformance numbers match the CSVs, but the record's 'prettify 1.17x vs nlohmann' compares Parson's compact serializer (harness bug) with nlohmann's indented dump, so I dropped it; tier A stays for the parse win over JsonCpp/json-c. Shortcomings to record: no project speed claim, parse win confined mostly to canada.json, slower than nlohmann/cJSON/RapidJSON, stringify slowest bar Qt, prettify row void, conformance failures, 2016 data.
